newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Bay, scene of Japan's worst oil spill.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Bay, scene of Japan's worst oil spill.

text.p: Tokyo Bay, scene of Japan's worst oil spill on Wednesday, is surrounded by a belt of industrial complexes, the major ports of Yokohama, Tokyo and Chiba, and is the country's busiest body of water next to Japan's capital.

The bay, an inlet of the Pacific Ocean, borders on the three highly populated prefectures of Kanagawa, Tokyo and Chiba with a combined population of 25.7 million people, more than one-fifth of Japan's total population.
A heavy traffic of tankers, freighters, ferry boats and fishing boats are controlled by a sophisticated navigation system aided by computers, radars and satellite telemetry to avoid collisions.

The supertanker Diamond Grace struck Nakanose reef, one of Tokyo Bay's best-known maritime hazards, in calm seas and clear weather. At its shallowest point, the reef is just 12 metres (39 feet) below the surface.
The bay is also next to Tokyo's main domestic airport at Haneda, the nation's busiest air terminal.
Two huge industrial complexes consisting of chemical and oil refineries as well as thermal power plants sprawl along the coasts of Kawasaki and Chiba on either side of the bay.

Oil fences have sprung up to protect oil from contaminating coolant sea water at the 11 thermal power plants that dot the bayshore, operated by Tokyo Electric Power Co. There are no nuclear power plants on the bay.

The development of industrial complexes began to replace farming and fishing along the bay in the late 1890s. The industrial zone between Tokyo and Yokohama was the target of some of the heaviest U.S. bombing during World War Two.

But despite its industrial image, there still are a small number of fishermen who annually catch some 20,000 tonnes of choice fish and shell fish, including flounders, ark shells and sea urchins that are often used for sushi.
Two large rivers, the Sumida and Tama, flow into Tokyo Bay.
The U.S. aircraft carrier Independence is homeported in Yokosuka at the mouth of the bay, the largest U.S. Navy base in Japan. Yokosuka is also home to the Japanese navy.

In recent years, the Tokyo Bay area has featured the construction of resort facilities including artificial beaches, seaside malls, posh bars, restaurants and hotels following the opening of Tokyo Disneyland in 1983.
